item.title: Tucson Twinkling at Twilight
item.description:
On 30 August 2026, NSF NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador Hernán Stockebrand captured this view of Tucson, Arizona, after sunset. On the far right, peeking up over the Quinlan Mountains, is the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory, a Program of NSF NOIRLab. 

Amazingly, this picture was captured about 60 miles (96.6 km) away from Kitt Peak, from Windy Point Vista off the Catalina Highway. Windy Point Vista is an iconic Tucson site, and stopping to enjoy the views above the city is a must before you continue up the Catalina Highway to its end at Mount Lemmon. Both Mount Lemmon and Kitt Peak are considered “Sky Islands” — a term for the unique diversity of plants and animals on these isolated mountains compared to the desert “seas” below. For example, the Sonoran Desert below both mountains is home to Saguaro cacti. As you drive up Kitt Peak, temperatures cool, and patches of cacti give way to lush trees, bushes, and grass unlike anywhere below. 

To spot more iconic Tucson locations in these images, see the annotated version here. You can find another angle of this view here.

item.title: Earthly Expanse Around Rubin
item.description:
This unique view can only be seen by looking northwest from the very top of the dome of NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. With clear skies above and the sprawling foothills of the Chilean Andes below, Rubin gives us a front-row seat to magnificent views of Earth and the cosmos. Rubin Observatory is jointly funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science (DOE/SC). In the center of the distant mountain peak, you can also see the silver dome of the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, part of the NSF Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

Chile is a great place to collect high-quality astronomical observations not only due to its arid climate and dark skies, but also its advanced infrastructure. The local governments of Coquimbo and La Serena facilitated safe transport of huge pieces of Rubin’s equipment through populated areas during construction of the summit facility. Data from Rubin travels through the national fiber-optic network of the Research and Education Network of Chile (REUNA). Chile has some of the fastest fixed-broadband internet speeds in the world, which observatories rely on to send their data to researchers and the public around the world. For Rubin specifically, this extensive infrastructure allows data to be sent from Cerro Pachón to SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in California for processing within about seven seconds of image capture. Thanks to these important partnerships, Rubin and Chile are ready to capture the cosmos.
